title: Tinman terminal object model
description: The semantic reading of a rendered virtual screen: nested rectangles carrying roles, names, text and the presentation they were drawn with. This is the terminal's equivalent of the browser document object model, and it is what locators bind against. Structure and presentation are both carried, for the same reason a browser exposes a computed style beside the element tree: a test author asserting that a warning line is drawn in red is asking about the screen, not about the program's internals, and a model that drops the cell attributes cannot answer them. Tinman reads an attributed cell grid and derives roles from those attributes, so the attributes are already in hand; carrying them costs nothing and withholding them pushes every presentation assertion into a bespoke check against the raw grid. Referenced by features/terminal-object-model.feature, features/tom-inference.feature and features/inspect-command.feature.

rows.description: Height of the screen the model was built from.

cols.description: Width of the screen the model was built from.

cursor.description: Where the terminal's cursor stands, the model's equivalent of the browser's caret. A program that is taking input puts the cursor where the next character will land, and an operator reads that position to learn whether the program is listening; a model that omits it cannot answer the first question anyone asks of an input. Absent only where the program has hidden the cursor, which is itself the observable difference between a screen that takes input and one that does not.
A cell position on the screen, counted from the top left.

colour.description: One cell colour. "default" is the terminal's own foreground or background, which is what a program that sets no colour leaves behind, and it is distinct from a named colour that happens to render the same way: a program setting white on a white-on-black terminal has done something the operator can see under a different theme, and the model says so. A named colour is one of the sixteen the terminal palette names. Anything else is reported as the program set it, by palette index or by channel, because Tinman reports what was drawn rather than guessing which name was meant.

style.description: The presentation every cell of a region shares, the terminal's equivalent of a computed style. Every key is stated rather than omitted when it holds its default, so a locator asserting a colour reads one shape whatever the program set: a region drawn plainly reports the default foreground and the default background rather than reporting nothing. A region whose cells disagree carries no style at all, and that absence is the honest answer: a single computed style for a region drawn two ways would be a summary, and a test author asserting against a summary is asserting against Tinman rather than against the screen.

rect.description: A Ratatui-shaped rectangle in screen cells.

region.description: One node of the model. A region owns a rectangle of the screen and may split into child regions.

role.description: The semantic role the region plays on screen, drawn from the WAI-ARIA role taxonomy at https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#role_definitions. Tinman coins no roles of its own: a role assistive technology already understands is one a test author already understands, and the taxonomy carries containment expectations Tinman would otherwise invent, such as a listitem belonging to a list and a menuitem to a menu. The root region is `application`, ARIA's role for a widget region whose keystrokes the program interprets rather than the terminal. This set holds the roles a scenario exercises today; a role is added when a scenario needs it, not in anticipation.

name.description: The accessible name a locator matches, such as a pane title or an item's label.

text.description: The region's rendered text, with trailing blanks removed.

selected.description: Whether the region is the currently selected or highlighted one among its siblings.

style.description: The presentation the region is drawn with, absent where its cells disagree.

allOf.description: WAI-ARIA 1.2 divides the roles this model produces into those supporting a name from the author and those requiring one. A region carrying a role from the required set and no name is a region a screen reader announces by role alone, which is the flat-text failure this model exists to close. The roles left out are not oversights: menu, list, listitem, status, log and article support a name without requiring one, so demanding it here would contradict the specification the model borrows its vocabulary from.
